1w9gwro:227: The blind-test Comparator in Layer 3 is the most ingeniously designed part of the entire system. In traditional A/B testing, the evaluator knowing which is the “experimental group” creates systematic bias—being either stricter or more lenient toward the experimental group. The blind-test design fundamentally removes this source of bias. But blind testing is only a means; the real value lies in the attribution process after the Analyzer unblinds: the Comparator gives a score, and the Analyzer explains “why with_skill won/lost.” This two-layer structure of “scoring + attribution” turns evaluation conclusions from a mere “good/bad” verdict into actionable “improvement suggestions.”

Forcibly separating the raw tool-call records from the AI's subjective explanations ensures that the Grader always looks at the system facts first, then listens to the AI's interpretation. The rule "if only agent_notes support it, with no tool_calls corroborating → forced FAIL" turns this constraint into an unbypassable hard rule, rather than a negotiable soft suggestion.

9xilxc:259: The separation of Layer 2a and Layer 2b is one of the most critical design decisions in the entire system. Field-exact validation (Ground Truth) completely excludes LLM from making judgments, ensuring that verification of objective facts such as interface call counts and parameter values is not polluted by subjective factors; Layer 2b, in turn, uses an independent Grader Agent to handle semantic and subjective judgments. The boundary between the two layers (objective vs. subjective) is not artificially drawn, but determined by the essential nature of the problem. In practice, the reason many evaluation systems fail is precisely that they mix verifications that should be layered—wanting the LLM to make semantic judgments while also wanting the same LLM to perform exact-value validation, resulting in the two types of judgments interfering with each other.
